title: The last night of the world
saying: aeternamque illam et novissimam noctem mundō
author: Pliny the Younger
setting: The road out of Misenum, AD 79

source_text: Vix consideramus, et nox - non qualis illunis aut nubila, sed qualis in locis clausis lumine exstincto. Audires ululatus feminarum, infantum quiritatus, clamores virorum; alii parentes alii liberos alii coniuges vocibus requirebant, vocibus noscitabant; hi suum casum, illi suorum miserabantur; erant qui metu mortis mortem precarentur; multi ad deos manus tollere, plures nusquam iam deos ullos aeternamque illam et novissimam noctem mundo interpretabantur.
excerpt_note: All of 6.20.14 and the first sentence of 6.20.15. The Perseus text ends 6.20.14 with a semicolon and begins 6.20.15 in lower case; the sentence runs on across the section break. The dash after nox is a spaced hyphen in the file; there is no closing dash.

translation: We had barely sat down when night came on: not a night with no moon or with clouds, but like the dark of a shut room when the lamp has been put out. You could have heard women wailing, babies crying, men shouting. People were calling for their parents, their children, their husbands or wives, and trying to tell them apart by their voices. Some grieved over what was happening to them, others over what was happening to their families; there were people who, out of fear of death, prayed to die. Many lifted their hands to the gods; more concluded that there were no gods anywhere any more, and that this was the everlasting, final night of the world.
translation_note: Vix cōnsīderāmus looks like the present of cōnsīderō ("consider"), but Lewis & Short file this very passage (Plin. Ep. 6, 20, 14) under cōnsīdō, "sit down", whose perfect is cōnsēdī or cōnsīdī: so it is the pluperfect, "we had (barely) sat down" (Lewis & Short, Perseus TEI, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PerseusDL/lexica/master/CTS_XML_TEI/perseus/pdllex/lat/ls/lat.ls.perseus-eng1.xml). Audīrēs is a potential subjunctive ("you would have heard"). tollere is a historical infinitive, used like a past tense. The last clause is indirect statement: deōs (esse) nusquam, "that the gods were nowhere".

essay.t: Tacitus, having read Pliny's letter about his uncle, asked what Pliny himself had gone through after staying behind at Misenum, and this second letter answers.
Pliny introduces it with a line Aeneas speaks before telling of the fall of Troy, quamquam animus meminisse horret (Aeneid 2.12): "though my mind shudders to remember".
He says he was in his eighteenth year and, with what he calls either composure or foolishness, sat reading Livy and making excerpts.
When the danger grew, his mother begged him to escape without her, since she was old and heavy; he refused and made her hurry along with him.
A dense darkness followed them, spreading over the land like a torrent, and the darkness and panic of this passage fell on the crowd on the road.
The USGS notes that the eruption produced pyroclastic flows and surges as well as heavy ashfall; linking Pliny's moving cloud to such a flow is my inference, not his.
Pliny reports rumours too: people adding invented terrors to real dangers, and messengers announcing, falsely but to believing ears, that Misenum had collapsed or was in flames.
He says he could boast that no groan escaped him, were it not that he believed he and the whole world were dying together, which he calls a wretched but great comfort.
When daylight returned, the sun was pale as in an eclipse and everything lay under ash like snow; the family went back to Misenum and waited for news of the uncle.
He ends by telling Tacitus that he will read these things, not at all worthy of history, without intending to write them up.
That modesty may be literary: Pliny wrote the letter at Tacitus' request and published it in his own collection, and its vivid scenes are carefully composed.

questions.q: What did many people in the crowd conclude, according to Pliny?
options: That there were no gods and this was the last night
That the gods would soon end the darkness
That the emperor's ships would rescue them
That the cloud came from a fire in Misenum

questions.q: What does the darkness remind Pliny of?
options: A shut room when the lamp is put out
A night with no moon and no stars
A cloudy night out at sea
The smoke of a burning city

questions.q: How does Pliny frame the whole letter at its start?
options: With Aeneas' words before the fall of Troy
With a line from his uncle's Natural History
With a prayer to the god Vulcan
With the date and hour of the eruption
